as_told: In 1997 Apple was weeks from bankruptcy. Bill Gates's Microsoft put $150 million into Apple, and that money saved the company. Without its great rival's cash, there would be no iMac, iPod or iPhone.
lesson: A rival's cash injection can be what keeps a failing company alive.
what_happened: In August 1997 Apple and Microsoft signed patent cross-licence and technology agreements. Microsoft agreed to make Office and Internet Explorer for the Mac OS for five years, Apple agreed to bundle Internet Explorer as the default browser, and Microsoft bought 150,000 shares of non-voting convertible preferred stock for $150 million. Apple's 10-K for the year to 26 September 1997 shows $1,459 million in cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments on that date; this figure already includes the $150 million, so Apple held about $1.3 billion without it. In the same filing Apple said its cash, short-term investments and bank borrowings would be sufficient for the next twelve months, though its debt was rated below investment grade and it had lost $1,045 million in the year.
false_part: The $150 million was about a tenth of the cash Apple already held, and Apple's own filing did not describe it as what kept the company out of bankruptcy.
